Unit  16
          16.1
                    | =   the gardening article you gave me and then passed it on to a friend who’s also interested in
                  1
                    plants.
                  2 Do you think she’s really angry, or do you think she’s just putting it on?
                  3 He looks very pale and tired. Something is clearly weighing on him.
                    Or Something is clearly weighing on his mind.
                  4 It’s a lovely jacket. Try it on.
                  5    going to keep on working until I’ve finished this report.
                  6 You can rely/depend/count on William.
          16.2
                  1 False, because keep on means to continue to do something, and Anwar has decided to tell Oscar
                    the news tomorrow.
                 2        because take in means to reduce the width of a piece of clothing, and Alice’s skirt was too
                    oose.
                 3  True
                 4  True
                 5  False, because count on means rely on, and Edward has been able to rely on his parents’ support.
                 6  True
         16.3
                 1  Hey, that man just pushed in - that taxi should have been ours!
                 2  Heidi’s bad news has been weighing on my mind all day.
                 3  | need time for the news to sink in.
                 4  | couldn’t leave the room because someone had locked me in. (You are locked out of a room if you
                    cannot get in.)
                 5  Phrasal verbs may seem hard but you must keep on trying.
                 6       never guess who called in at the office today!
                 Over to you
                 Possible answers:
                 pass on =die
                 e.g. I’m so sorry to hear that your dad has passed on.
                 take in = let someone stay in your house
                 e.g. She took me in for a month while the building work was done on my house.
                 rub sth in (informal) = talk to someone about something which you know they want
                 to forget because they feel bad about it
                 e.g. | know | shouldn’t have failed the exams, but there’s no need to keep rubbing it in.

                 Unit  17
                   We  know that Jamie’s luggage is heavy and/or that there is a lot of it.
         17.1
                 1
                   Yes, but she’s trying to eat less chocolate than she used to. Though she would probably be quite
                 2
                   happy  if she could cut it out totally. [stop eating it completely]
                   He wrote it rather than remembered it.
                 3
                   No, it has closed permanently, not just for the evening.
                 4
                   Perhaps they did it because the bushes were so big that they were blocking the light or blocking
                 5
                   the path.
                   shut     2 cut    3  hand    4  chopped     5 keep     6 go
         17.2
                   Read through, look through and go through are all possible. Using through perhaps suggests more
         17.3
                   thoroughness than over, which can be quite superficial. However, the difference is very slight.
                   They all share an idea of change or of moving from one state or time to another:
                   stay over = staying from one day to the next
                   get over = change from feeling bad to feeling better
                   fall over = change from a vertical to a horizontal position
                   a) heaviness which causes difficulty
                   b) put on paper or onan electronic device

                                                               English Phrasal Verbs in Use Intermediate   153
